Start: 15:00 UTC

Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Romero (Redwood SE), John Lewis (ACME ML), Priya Singh (ACME Infra), Carlos Mendez (ACME Platform)
Recording: Fireflies auto-transcript (medium quality)

summary: Deep technical review of quantization options (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) focused on accuracy regressions, runtime perf (latency/throughput), KV cache interactions, batching strategies, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Customer emphasized strict 95th percentile latency SLO of 120 ms for short prompts and need for private deployment with KMS. Redwood SE proposed AWQ for best latency with minimal regressions on ACME prompts, but agreed to run full head-to-head on their corpuses. Action items and next steps captured.
topics: KV cache behavior with quantized models
Batching and continuous batching impact on tail latency
transcript:
[00:00:00] Sam Patel (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call, and then we'll hand over to Maya for the quantization deep dive.
[00:00:28] John Lewis (ACME): Hi, John here. We got a couple of folks on end but main attendees are me and Priya. Our main ask is, can we get down to the numbers for AWQ vs GPTQ and understand any accuracy delta for our rerank and support prompts?
[00:00:45] Maya Chen (Redwood SE): Yep, perfect. I'll share my screen in a sec — but quick topo: we'll run through INT8 vs FP8 primers, then GPTQ/AWQ internals, show perf numbers on our internal rig, then discuss KV cache interactions and batching.
[00:01:10] Priya Singh (ACME Infra): Quick infra note — we need this to run on our VPC, ideally private control plane. Encryption in transit and KMS at rest are hard requirements.
[00:01:27] Sam: Noted, Priya. We'll cover how Redwood Private handles KMS/HSM and audit logs.
[00:01:40] Luis Romero (Redwood SE): Starting slides — INT8 gives the biggest size / speed wins but has quant noise; FP8 (if supported) keeps more dynamic range and often yields fewer regression cases.
[00:02:05] Carlos Mendez (ACME): When you say 'regressions' do you mean semantic drift on long-form answers, or more ranking accuracy hits? For us, rerank delta is most critical.
[00:02:22] Maya: Good clarification — for rerank we look at pairwise accuracy / MRR. In our internal tests, INT8 (non-GPTQ) sometimes changes top-1 for ~2-3% of items on a few workloads; GPTQ reduces that but sometimes misses edge tokens. AWQ is an alternative quant scheme that preserves accuracy better on sparse heads — in our experiments AWQ matched FP16 accuracy within margin on many classification/rerank prompts.
[00:02:55] John: 2-3% top-1 is concerning. What was seq length and temperature?
[00:03:08] Maya: Mostly short prompts, seq len ~64, temp 0.0 for rerank scoring. We also ran a couple tests at temp 0.7 for generative quality checks.
[00:03:25] [00:03:30] Sam: Quick interjection — when you say AWQ matched FP16, are those cherry-picked? We need to see head-to-head with ACME prompts.
[00:03:42] Maya: Totally — these were internal. That's why the next step is for you to drop your prompt sets so we can run the same pipeline.
[00:03:55] Priya: Also curious how KV cache behaves — does quantization change cache hit semantics or memory layout causing more cache misses?
[00:04:10] Luis: Great Q. Mechanically, KV cache stores key/value tensors; quantization affects tensor storage precision and packing. With AWQ and GPTQ we see smaller memory footprint so larger effective cache capacity which can improve hit rates, but misalignment in block sizes can cause slight perf jitter.
[00:04:35] John: So potentially better cache capacity but jitter in latency? We have a 95th pct SLO of 120 ms for short inference.
[00:04:47] Maya: Right — throughput can go up, avg latency down, but tail can be sensitive to batching and cache eviction policies. We recommend continuous batching with small max batch size and latency-aware cutoff to protect 95th percentile.
[00:05:10] [00:05:40] Maya: I'm going to show some numbers from our 8x A100 tests. Baseline FP16 avg token latency 6.2 ms, INT8 avg token latency ~3.8 ms, AWQ ~3.9 ms but with slightly better per-sequence accuracy than INT8. 95th pct for FP16 was 22 ms, INT8 40 ms, AWQ 28 ms in this setup (note: these are token-level numbers, real request latency multiplies by tokens).
[00:06:15] Carlos: Those 95th numbers jump a lot for INT8 — why so high?
[00:06:23] Luis: Likely due to quant kernel fallback and memory fetch patterns — some kernels are not fused for specific layer dims causing spikes. AWQ's packing avoids that in many models.
[00:06:40] John: Can you run this on our infra? I want to see end-to-end with our VPC egress and model pinned to dedicated pool.
[00:06:52] Sam: Yes, we can run dedicated reserved capacity with pinned model versions. For private deployments we'll package similar kernels but may need to tune GPU kernels for your specific hardware, esp if you use older gen.
[00:07:12] Priya: Our environment is a mix of on-prem 80GB GPUs and some GCP A2, could that variability cause different regressions?
[00:07:25] Maya: Absolutely — kernel availability, CUDA versions, and tensor core behavior vary. GPTQ/AWQ artifacts are somewhat hardware-specific; we supply a per-node kernel compatibility matrix. We'll include that in the deliverables.
[00:07:43] [00:08:00] Sam: Let's talk accuracy: what magnitude of drop is acceptable for ACME?
[00:08:08] John: For rerank MRR we can't drop more than 0.5% absolute. For support responses, some fuzz is ok but we need predictable behavior.
[00:08:19] Maya: Understood. From our internal, AWQ often stays within 0.2% of FP16 on rerank MRR for many models; GPTQ varies — sometimes within 0.3-0.6% depending on the calibration. INT8 without fine tuning can exceed 1% in fragile workloads.
[00:08:40] Carlos: What's calibration? Do you fine-tune or do post-training calibrations?
[00:08:50] Luis: For GPTQ there is a calibration step that uses a representative dataset to compute quant step sizes; some GPTQ variants require per-channel calibration. AWQ often uses adaptive block quantization with optional calibration. We typically run calibration with ~10k tokens from target domain.
[00:09:12] Priya: If calibration needs customer data, any privacy concerns? We operate in regulated verticals.
[00:09:22] Maya: We can run calibration inside your VPC on your data; Redwood Private supports local-only calibration flows and we don't persist raw data outside your environment. KMS is used for model artifacts and any persisted metrics.
[00:09:40] [00:10:05] John: How does batching affect tail latency in practice? We have bursty traffic.
[00:10:15] Maya: Continuous batching improves throughput by combining small requests, but it introduces a batching delay. We recommend dynamic batching with a short max wait (e.g., 5-10 ms) and a small max batch size (e.g., 8) for your 120 ms SLO. Also KV cache prefix caching reduces tokens per request which helps.
[00:10:38] Sam: Also Redwood has smart routing — if Dedicated pool is under pressure we can fall back to hosted compatible model variants to preserve latency.
[00:10:50] Carlos: Any known issues with AWQ on long-sequence caching or attention?
[00:11:00] Luis: In some models with fused attention kernels, AWQ quant blocks lead to less efficient fused path, leading to a small perf penalty at longer seq lengths. For your primary workloads with seq < 256 it's usually fine.
[00:11:18] [00:11:35] Maya: I'm switching to live demo — raw numbers from our sanbox: run A, FP16 baseline, run B GPTQ, run C AWQ. I'll read off a couple of rows: "prompt set alpha" (rerank): FP16 MRR 0.842, GPTQ 0.837, AWQ 0.840; latency p95 full request FP16 110 ms, GPTQ 145 ms, AWQ 125 ms on this cluster.
[00:12:05] John: That suggests GPTQ increased p95 — likely because of kernel fallbacks?
[00:12:15] Luis: Yes, on that cluster the GPTQ kernels weren't fully fused so some layers did a fallback to generic kernels. It depends on tensor dims and CUDA libraries.
[00:12:28] Priya: We asked about FP8 — is that available? What's the story?
[00:12:36] Maya: FP8 is promising and preserves dynamic range but requires HW/driver support. On A100+ with recent runtimes you can enable experimental FP8 paths; we treat FP8 as near-FP16 accuracy with better speed, but it's not yet as battle-tested in our stack. It's an option if you control your HW stack fully.
[00:12:58] [00:13:20] Sam: We're hearing two themes — accuracy preservation (esp for rerank MRR) and 95th pct latency. Proposed short plan: run head-to-head AWQ vs GPTQ vs FP16 across your two corpuses; collect MRR/accuracy, AVG/95 latency, and kernel fallback logs.
[00:13:40] John: Agree. How long will runs take? We want results quickly.
[00:13:48] Maya: If you give us prompts and a small calibration set we can run baseline + two quant variants in ~24-48 hours on Redwood infra; for on-prem we might need extra compute tuning and that could be 2-3 days.
[00:14:05] Carlos: About KV cache again — does Redwood persist cache across warm starts? We rely on prefix caching across sessions for multi-turn agents.
[00:14:17] Luis: We persist KV cache per session when session affinity is enabled; on quantized models we store packed tensors. We recommend TTL-based cache eviction and sticky routing to keep the same worker for session lifespan.
[00:14:36] Priya: If cache is persisted to disk, encryption at rest?
[00:14:42] Maya: Yes, in Private deployments KV cache shards can be encrypted with your KMS keys. No cache shards leave your VPC unless you opt into cross-region replication.
[00:14:57] [00:15:20] John: Any known edge regressions for AWQ on generation tasks, like hallucination increases?
[00:15:28] Luis: We haven't observed systematic hallucination increases with AWQ vs FP16; most generation quality differences are content-specific. AWQ tends to preserve logits distribution better than naive INT8. That said, we'll need to validate on your support prompts.
[00:15:45] Maya: I'm uploading the benchmark CSV link now (shows link in chat). The CSV includes token-level latencies, kernel names per layer, and a regression flag.
[00:15:58] [00:16:20] Sam: On the security side, Priya, our Private mode supports customer-managed keys, MFA for console, RBAC, and full audit trails. For SOC2 we can share the package.
[00:16:35] Priya: Good, we will need SOC2 + ISO docs and encryption attestation.
[00:16:42] Sam: We'll attach those to the follow-up.
[00:16:50] [00:17:10] John: Can you also include the exact kernel versions and CUDA driver we used? We need to reproduce locally.
[00:17:18] Maya: Yes, benchmark artifact includes driver, CUDA, cuDNN, and library build tags. We also log fused kernel names when used.
[00:17:30] Carlos: For the head-to-head runs, will Redwood simulate our production traffic pattern (bursty)?
[00:17:38] Luis: We can run a synthetic workload with your TTL, burst profile, and a sticky routing policy so tail latency numbers reflect real behavior.
[00:17:52] [00:18:10] John: About model rollout — if AWQ works, can we do canary on small percent of traffic?
[00:18:19] Sam: Yes, Redwood Console supports canary rollouts and A/B evaluation. We can route 5% to AWQ then expand with automatic rollback if quality regressions exceed threshold.
[00:18:34] Priya: Is there any performance regression on cold starts after model swap?
[00:18:42] Maya: Cold starts depend on model load time and kernel warmup. Quantized artifacts are smaller so load time often faster, but if we need to JIT or compile kernels at first run that can add a one-time penalty. We recommend pre-warming within the Dedicated pool.
[00:18:59] [00:19:20] Sam: Quick pause — any other questions from ACME before we get into the more detailed kernel logs?
[00:19:26] John: One more — for privacy, can we run the calibration step entirely on our cluster without Redwood seeing outputs?
[00:19:33] Maya: Yes, we have an offline calibration package and a script that runs locally and emits quant params; you can then upload only the quant parameters to Redwood.
[00:19:47] Carlos: That helps.
[00:19:55] [00:20:10] Maya: Moving into kernel log view... (reads) Layer 3 fallback to generic_matmul kernel on GPTQ run — this correlated with p95 spike. For AWQ we saw a packed_sgemm fused kernel.
[00:20:35] John: Are there licensing implications for AWQ/GPTQ toolchains?
[00:20:43] Luis: GPL/licensing depends on the exact patch; our packaging uses permissive runtime libraries and we provide license manifests. We'll include a license summary.
[00:20:57] Priya: Good. On ops — how do model artifacts version and pinning work with quantized variants?
[00:21:07] Maya: You can pin model version + quant profile. We treat quant profile as an artifact and version it; rollbacks are atomic to previous quant profile.
[00:21:18] [00:21:50] Sam: OK, time check — about 50 minutes left. Maya, any notable anomalies you want ACME to be aware of?
[00:21:59] Maya: Two items: 1) some GPTQ converters produce slightly different per-channel scales depending on calibration seed; always run deterministic seed and log seeds. 2) AWQ often needs block-size tuning per model; our default works for many but we tune for best MRR.
[00:22:22] John: Seed determinism — we'll want that reproducible in our pipelines.
[00:22:27] Luis: We'll hand you the reproducible script.
[00:22:35] [00:23:00] Maya: I'm going to outline the exact experiment we'll run for you: dataset split, calibration subset, metrics (MRR, top-1, avg latency, p95, kernel fallback count, cache hit rate). We'll push the YAML to the shared drive.
[00:23:18] John: Sounds good.
[00:23:25] Priya: For Private deployment, do you provide manifests for our infra-as-code?
[00:23:33] Sam: Yes, Terraform modules and Helm charts are available; we'll attach the sample for your hybrid cluster.
[00:23:44] [00:24:05] Carlos: Any recommended quant profile for our use-case if we want conservative approach?
[00:24:12] Maya: Conservative: FP16 -> AWQ with block-size tuned, calibration on 10k domain tokens, dynamic batching with max wait 8 ms, sticky routing with session affinity. That tends to be safe for both rerank and support generation.
[00:24:30] John: Let's capture that as the initial config.
[00:24:34] Sam: Noted.
[00:24:40] [00:25:05] Maya: Last bits — I will run a smoke test today on our infra using your provided calibration subset once you drop it. Expect CSV + logs in 24-48 hours.
[00:25:18] John: We'll upload prompts by EOD tomorrow.
[00:25:23] Priya: And I'll review the Private/VPC checklist.
[00:25:28] Sam: Great. Recap and next steps in chat. Thanks all.
[01:15:00] Meeting concluded.
